content:
Arthritis itself does not make bones break, but several things that come with it can raise your fracture risk. These include falls from pain, stiffness or weak muscles, long-term steroid tablets, inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, and being less active. The good news is that much of that risk can be reduced, and your GP can assess it.

Arthritis and osteoporosis are different

Arthritis affects joints. Osteoporosis is a loss of bone strength that makes bones fragile. The two are often confused, and many people have both. Osteoporosis has no symptoms until a bone breaks, which is why checking your risk matters.

Why fracture risk can be higher with arthritis

Falls. Painful knees or hips, stiff ankles, poor balance and weaker leg muscles all make trips and falls more likely. Most fractures in older adults happen after a fall from standing height.

Steroids. Taking steroid tablets such as prednisolone for three months or more can thin bones. NICE (CG146) lists long-term steroid use as a reason to assess fracture risk.

Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory conditions. Ongoing inflammation affects bone. RA is one of the factors included in the FRAX fracture risk tool used by GPs.

Being less active. Bones need load to stay strong. When pain stops you moving, bones and muscles both weaken.

Other factors. Age, being female and past menopause, low body weight, smoking, drinking a lot of alcohol, a family history of hip fracture and a previous fracture all add to risk.

Common fractures to know about

  • Wrist — often from putting a hand out when falling
  • Hip — usually after a fall in later life. This is a serious injury that needs emergency care.
  • Spine (vertebral) fractures — can happen with little or no injury. They may show as sudden back pain, loss of height or a more curved upper back.
  • Upper arm and pelvis

Signs a bone may be broken

After a fall or knock, suspect a fracture if there is:

  • pain that is severe or getting worse, especially with movement or weight-bearing
  • swelling or bruising that develops quickly
  • a limb that looks bent, shortened or turned outwards
  • being unable to stand, walk or use the arm
  • sudden, severe back pain, even without a clear injury, if you have osteoporosis or take steroids

People with arthritis sometimes assume new pain is "just the arthritis". If pain is different, sudden or follows a fall, get it checked.

Getting your risk assessed

Ask your GP about a fracture risk assessment if you are over 50 and have arthritis plus any of the risks above, especially long-term steroids or a previous fracture. NICE recommends using a tool such as FRAX or QFracture. A DEXA bone density scan may be offered depending on the result.

If your risk is high, treatment to protect your bones may be offered. Your GP will explain the options and any checks needed.

Reducing your risk

  • Keep moving. Weight-bearing activity such as walking, plus strength and balance exercise, helps bones and lowers fall risk. Tai chi and strength-and-balance classes are good options.
  • Make your home safer. Good lighting, especially at night, grab rails, and removing loose rugs and clutter all help.
  • Review your medicines. Some tablets cause dizziness or drowsiness. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a medicines review, particularly if you take several.
  • Eat for bone health. Include calcium-rich foods and protein. Follow NHS advice on vitamin D, including the autumn and winter supplement advice. Your GP may advise more if you are at high risk.
  • Limit alcohol and stop smoking.
  • Check eyesight and feet. Wear well-fitting shoes with good grip.
  • Ask about steroids. If you need long-term steroids, ask whether bone protection is needed. Never stop steroids suddenly yourself.

After a fracture

A fracture after a minor fall is sometimes called a "fragility fracture" and is a signal to check for osteoporosis. Ask your GP or the fracture team whether this has been done. Many areas have a fracture liaison service. You can also ask for a falls assessment, which NICE (NG249) recommends after a fall.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
